name: git
description: Run sandboxed git commands on the project. Input: {"args": ["status", "--porcelain"]}. Allowed: status, diff, log, show, add, commit, ls-files, rev-parse, branch, worktree. push, reset, rebase, checkout, clean, rm, fetch, merge, revert, stash are denied by default; setting agent.git_remote_ops lifts push, merge and checkout for git. Runs at the run's root, the same directory the file tools resolve paths against, so plain `add`/`commit` stage exactly the files you edited. Git global options that take a value (-C <path>, --work-tree <path>) are honored, but only for paths inside the run's own tree: an argument naming .clanker-worktrees, or stepping above the run's root with .., is refused, because it would reach another run's worktree. Config-injection and alternate-git-dir options are refused outright (-c, --config-env, --git-dir, --git-common-dir, --exec-path): -c core.hooksPath=<dir> executes hook scripts on commit, core.fsmonitor/core.sshCommand/core.editor/core.pager/credential.helper/diff.external spawn config-named programs (on git before 2.43 alias.* could also shadow a builtin verb with a ! shell command), so those flags are a code-execution grant, and a git dir other than the run's own .git can carry a hook that runs on commit. Do not try to isolate your own work by adding a worktree and pointing git at it: only git would move, the file tools would not, so your edits would keep landing in the run's root while `git -C <wt> status` reported that worktree as clean. Isolation is the harness's (clanker run --worktree), and when it is on, the run's root already IS the worktree, addressed as `.`. Returns {"ok": bool, "code": int, "stdout": "...", "stderr": "..."}.
